items.value: A well-known survivalist meets their fate while filming their latest extreme adventure.

In the early hours of Tuesday morning, the unthinkable happened. Extreme adventurer and world-famous survival expert Wolf Mills (43) died while filming the latest edition of his extreme survival show Attack Life. News of his death may not have come as a surprise to many, as Wolf was known for jumping out of planes and dropping into the world's most remote and dangerous locations, all in the name of survival education. Referred to by some as a born survivor due to his ability to stare death in the face and come through it unscathed, it appears Wolf took things a step too far this time when he fell thousands of feet to his death. It is reported that he was sleeping on a portaledge (a portable platform rock climbers use to sleep on while ascending sheer rock faces) when the safety rope supporting him failed. It's understood that Wolf had a support team with him, who were camping on safer ground at the top of the plateau above. Investigations are underway to establish what caused the accident; however, the police have yet to rule out the possibility of foul play. For someone whose life was fueled by jeopardy and filled with life-threatening situations, plummeting to his death from a great height in the remote regions of Africa seems like a fittingly dramatic and adventurous way to go out. But I can't help but feel that there is more to this than meets the eye. Surely the indestructible Wolf Mills didn't meet his end due to something as simple as a faulty bit of kit?! Sandra Feldman, Crime Reporter & Co-host of the Murderous Mysteries podcast.

Summary of Incident: The victim's portaledge was secured to an overhang in the rock face at the top of a 2,000-foot cliff, where he went to sleep for the night. His teammates had set up a typical camp a few meters away atop the plateau. The next day, the victim's body was discovered at the base of the sheer rock face, still inside his sleeping bag. Found with him were his portaledge, head torch, climbing harness, and a large knife. Discovery: The victim's body was discovered at the base of the cliff the following day by his teammates. Time of Death: Sometime between 11:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m. Evidence Collected: - The broken safety rope, which had been used to secure the victim's portaledge to the cliff face, showed signs of being cut with a knife. - A large knife found at the base of the cliff, identified as belonging to the team's bush guide, was used to cut the rope. - Fingerprints of three of the victim's teammates were found on the knife. Further Details: Three of the victim's teammates are being questioned and treated as suspects, as their fingerprints were found on the knife used to cut the safety rope.

Q: How well did you know the victim? A: I've been his producer since the start of his TV career. When we first met, he was just another ex-military survival expert with minimal experience in front of the camera. But I worked my magic and turned him into a star. He brings adventure; I bring creativity and glamour. Q: Do you go with Wolf on all his travels? A: Not usually. Most of my work is done in a post-production studio, so I don't need to. But I went along sometimes, as it was a good way to maintain a close relationship with Wolf. Frankly, without the show Attack Life, my production company would be nothing, so keeping him happy was crucial. Q: Where was everyone the night Wolf died? A: The team camped on top of the plateau in our tents, apart from Wolf, who chose to sleep on a portaledge hanging off the top of the cliff. He told us that he slept better knowing there was a two-thousand-foot drop beneath him, classic Wolf. Q: How did you feel about Wolf sleeping on the cliff? A: I encouraged him. It added jeopardy to his journey, allowing us to give viewers the impression that Wolf had climbed the cliff to the plateau. I even gave him my personal video camera to take with him. I don't usually lend it to people, but I wanted him to make a video diary from bed with the drop beneath him; the shots would have been epic. Q: What do you think happened to Wolf? A: I don't like to speculate, but Paul's knife was found at the bottom, and the rope had been cut, so he is the prime suspect for me. Having said that, before coming on this trip, I'd heard rumblings of issues between Wolf and our camera operator, Dom. I felt the tension between them that evening. Dom made it clear that she was less than impressed with some of the dangerous situations Wolf had gotten her into that day.

Q: What was your relationship with Wolf? A: I'm part of his camera crew. It's my job to follow him on all his ridiculous adventures and film him surviving dangerous situations. I used to enjoy the work, but I must admit our relationship had become strained lately, and I had started looking for other jobs. Q: What caused your relationship to become strained? A: I was getting fed up with his careless attitude. It's one thing for him to come out to these remote areas and put himself into unnecessary danger for the sake of exciting TV. Still, he never considered the welfare of his crew, the people like me who had to blindly follow him as he climbed unstable cliffs, jumped from great heights into unknown water, and purposefully put himself in harm's way. He enjoyed living life on the edge and got paid a lot of money to do it. But I've had a few close calls filming him recently, and not once did Wolf show any concern for me or my young family at home. Q: Talk us through the night Wolf died? A: After a long day of filming, we camped at the top of a plateau. It was a beautiful spot with spectacular views. The four of us spent the evening around the campfire. Paul, our bush guide, had caught a kudu earlier in the day, which we all cooked on the fire and ate. Apart from Rupert, who's a vegetarian, he stuck with his bland boil-in-the-bag meal. After that, we went to our tents for the night, and Wolf climbed down onto his portaledge. I told him sleeping on the cliff was stupid and that I wouldn't be climbing down to film him. But he never listened. When we woke the next morning, we discovered that Wolf's safety rope must have failed during the night because he had fallen. Q: How did people react to the discovery that Wolf had fallen? A: It was surreal. Even on the climb down to find him, it still hadn't sunk in. Paul, the guide, was still making jokes about how reckless Wolf was, and Rupert was messing around with his video camera, taking shots of the sunrise. It wasn't until we got to the bottom and saw Wolf's body that reality hit us. We were so used to seeing Wolf in dangerous situations and always coming out of them unscathed that we had become immune to the fact that he was only human.

Q: How well did you know Wolf? A: I've worked with him a few times over the years. I'm a specialist bush guide, and when Wolf came to Africa to film, I'd take him and his crew around to get all the shots they needed. I can't say I enjoyed working with him, but the pay was good. Q: Why didn't you like working with him? A: Unfortunately, working with Wolf has damaged my reputation as a guide in the past. He had a reckless approach to survival, prioritizing an extreme appearance in front of the camera. Last year, on a bush walk, we came across a zebra carcass in the wild. I knew the meat was rotten, so I advised Wolf to leave it. But he thought it would make good TV and ignored me. He had his crew film him eating it raw as he talked about how, in extreme survival situations, you can never turn down the opportunity to eat. He ended up with severe food poisoning, and I had to call for an emergency evacuation. Word of such things spreads fast in my community, and it's damaging to your reputation. The worst part of that story is the scene still made it into his show, only with the emergency evacuation edited out. He was a poor role model. Q: What happened the night Wolf died? A: I taught the others how to prepare and cook a kudu on the campfire properly, then we all headed to bed at the same time. Wolf insisted on sleeping on the cliff face, hanging on his stupid portaledge. I told him it was a pointless exercise, but he and his producer were adamant that the footage would be good for the show. At dawn the next day, Wolf and his portaledge were gone. He must not have fastened his anchor securely enough into the rock. We found his remains at the base of the cliff. Q: Your bush knife was found at the base of the cliff with Wolf and his tent. Can you explain why? A: No, I can't explain that. We had all used the knife the night before to prepare and eat the kudu over the fire. I'd like to have it back, please? I thought I had lost it.

Key Evidence
- The police report confirms that all three suspects' fingerprints are on Paul's knife, which was used to cut the safety rope and cause the victim's death. Paul and Dom's fingerprints are explained as we know the evening before they used it to cook and eat a Kudu on the campfire. However, Rupert did not participate in this due to being a vegetarian; therefore, his fingerprints on the knife are not explained. - Rupert is the only suspect to encourage the victim to sleep, hanging off the cliff face. Both Dom and Paul had tried to dissuade him. - Rupert is the only suspect to refer to the rope being intentionally cut with a knife, information that is contained in the confidential police report. Both Paul and Dom refer to Wolf's death as if it were due to a personal error or faulty equipment. - Rupert tells us he gave the victim a camera to take to bed so they could make a video diary whilst hanging from the cliff face. However, the police report does not reference any such camera being found with the body at the bottom. If the victim had it, then it would have fallen with them. Dom references Rupert using the same camera the following morning on the climb down to find the victim's remains. If Rupert had the camera in the morning, he must have taken it back from the victim during the night, before they fell to their death.

Confession
I mentioned that I had heard rumblings of Wolf being dissatisfied with some of his film crew, but what I didn't tell you was that this included me. I came on this trip to try to reconnect with Wolf and resolve any issues, but unfortunately, I was too late. Earlier that day, he said that this would be his last show with me; apparently, he wanted to take his career in a different direction. My fear had come true. Attack Life was the only show making my production company any money, and nobody in the industry would take me seriously if the only talent I had dropped me to go elsewhere. When he said that he was going to hang his portaledge off the cliff that night and sleep with a 2,000-foot drop beneath him, it made me think. I concluded that my show's star dying dramatically would be far more palatable and less detrimental to my career than his firing me. Not only that, but the publicity and hype surrounding his death would likely send this season's viewing figures skyrocketing! I had the intention of unclipping Wolf's safety rope, but as I got up, I saw Paul's bush knife by the campfire, still there from dinner. I thought using it would be a clever way to put suspicion on him. As I leaned over the cliff edge to cut the rope, I saw my camera attached to it. Wolf must have rigged it up to take a time-lapse of his extreme night's camp. It's an expensive bit of kit, and I wasn't going to let it fall, so I unclipped it and took it back. Once the rope was cut, I watched Wolf in his sleep peacefully disappear down into the night sky. I threw Paul's knife down afterward to draw attention to the fact that it had been used.
